profile.summary: 2 John is the shortest letter of the New Testament and shows how principles already taught in 1 John - to remain in the truth, to love the brethren and to guard themselves from false teachers - must be applied to a concrete situation. The letter was written amid tensions in the churches of Asia Minor, where there were itinerant teachers propagating a wrong view of Jesus, especially denying his true humanity. The author urges the community to remain faithful to apostolic teaching, to live Christian love in an obedient way and not to offer support to those who distort the truth about Christ. The authorship is traditionally attributed to the apostle John, although some scholars have raised doubts; yet the letter is presented as part of the same Jordanian and pastoral circle.
profile.setting: The letter is probably located in Asia Minor, amidst churches under the care of John. The background is the performance of false teachers who circulated among the communities, teaching a mistaken doctrine about Jesus, especially his incarnation and true humanity. Part of the church seems to have been influenced by this teaching and departed from communion. The recipient is described as an elected "lady time," an expression that may indicate a woman and his family, but probably designates a local church and its members. The letter is personal, brief and pastoral, written to strengthen the community in truth and love.

structure.label: Brief letter of exhortation and warning
structure.description: Initial greeting, appeal to remain in truth and love, warns against false teachers and closure with expectation of visit and greetings.

themes: Faithfulness to the person of Jesus Christ
readingKeys: Notice how truth and love do not appear as opposites, but as inseparable realities in church life.
Note that the warning about false teachers is not abstract: it leads to practical decisions on reception, support and communion.
Read the letter as a concrete application of 1 John, realizing how its principles are put into action in a real situation.
profile.cautions: The exact authorship and identity of the recipients are debated by some scholars, although tradition attributes the letter to the apostle John. The source does not determine with certainty whether the elected "lord" is a specific person or a local church, so this question should be presented with caution. The text should also be read in the light of the doctrinal conflict of the period, without projecting details beyond what the introduction informs.

dossier.narratedEra: The narrated scenario is that of the Christian communities of Asia Minor, where itinerant masters circulated who denied that Jesus Christ came in real body. The letter presupposes churches that gathered in homes and a network of relationships between the apostle and their local communities. The text also presupposes a recipient described as "elected time" and her children, understood by the note as a local church and its members, although the reading of a specific woman is also mentioned.
dossier.compositionEra: The composition is located in the apostolic period, when John writes as the priest/elder and responds pastorally to a concrete crisis of heresy. The notes associate the letter with the time John was careful about various churches in Asia Minor. The exact date is not provided in the sources; the important thing for reading is that the letter is born as a brief and direct intervention against false masters, probably in continuity with the concerns already exposed in 1 John.

politics.title: Authority apostolic versus dissident masters
politics.detail: The letter counterposes the authority of John, who presents himself as an elder, to the influence of false teachers who have strayed from the apostolic teaching on Christ.
politics.readingImpact: Reading the letter as a dispute of authority helps to realize that the problem is not only doctrinal, but also of legitimacy: who can define the true teaching about Jesus?

politics.title: Intraecclesial conflict in Asia Minor
politics.detail: According to the introduction, some members, influenced by heresy, separated and formed a new group; the letter responds to this internal fracture in the churches of the region.
politics.readingImpact: This makes reading sound less like abstract controversy and more as an effort to preserve the communion of a community wounded by splitting.

politics.title: Absence of reference to external rulers
politics.detail: The notes do not discuss specific kings, emperors or civil authorities; the immediate political focus is ecclesial, non-state.
politics.readingImpact: The interpreter should not fill the letter with a detailed imperial scenario that the sources do not provide; the historical weight is in the internal governance of the church and in the dispute for doctrinal fidelity.

customs.title: Hospitality as community practice
customs.detail: The letter forbids receiving false teachers at home or in meetings, which presupposes that the churches were in homes and depended on hospitality for missionary functioning and worship.
customs.readingImpact: The reader realizes that hospitality, usually a Christian virtue, here needs to be discerned; welcoming the wrong is equivalent to participating in it.

customs.title: Christian meetings in homes
customs.detail: The note notes that the first churches gathered in houses, so the ban can mean both church meeting and domestic hospitality.
customs.readingImpact: This explains why the order is so concrete: the home was a space of worship, teaching and welcoming, so opening the door to the false master had direct ecclesial consequences.

customs.title: Brief communication on small material support
customs.detail: The introduction says that, in antiquity, the entire letter would fit on a papyrus leaf.
customs.readingImpact: The small size reinforces the reading of the epistle as a direct pastoral message, condensed and urgently practical.

customs.title: Recognition of a female recipient or a personified church
customs.detail: Matthew Henry points out that the epistle is primarily directed to a single female person; Tyndale also records the possibility of a specific woman named Kyria, although he considers a local personified church more likely.
customs.readingImpact: This prevents automatic reading and shows that the epistolary form can oscillate between individual and community; the application to the entire church remains plausible even when the greeting speaks as if it were for a lady.

customs.title: Afective fulfillment in Christian communion
customs.detail: The note in 1:12 explains that the desire to see "face to face" is an expression of full relationship between believers; the final greeting also brings the idea of complete joy in coexistence.
customs.readingImpact: The relational practice of the community is not optional: the letter values presence, visit and concrete communion, not just abstract belief.

language.title: Repetition of "truth" as a rhetorical axis
language.detail: The introduction notes that the word truth appears four times in the initial greeting and again in 1:4, showing that the letter unites doctrine and life.
language.readingImpact: The reader must treat "truth" not as a mere intellectual concept, but as the basis of Christian fidelity and mutual love.

language.title: Elder as a form of pastoral authority
language.detail: John identifies himself as an elder to assert authority in the church, according to the translation note.
language.readingImpact: Self-designation suggests a style of pastoral leadership and recognized, not a bureaucratic or state claim.

language.title: -Last time elected" / kyria
language.detail: The note highlights that the Greek kyria may be a woman's own name or reference to a local church and its members; Matthew Henry emphasizes the dignity of a female recipient.
language.readingImpact: This literary ambiguity guides reading: the letter can sound personal and, at the same time, ecclesial, without losing its community strength.

language.title: "Ir beyond and "not staying in teaching
language.detail: The expression of the note in 1:9 is glossated as going beyond the apostolic teaching and not remaining in it; that is, contradicting what the apostles taught about Jesus.
language.readingImpact: Vocabulary shows that the problem is not simple innovation, but rupture with the apostolic pattern; orthodoxy is defined by permanence.

language.title: "Mouth to mouth" / "face to face"
language.detail: The note reports that the Greek expression is literally "mouthed with mouth," equivalent to our face-to-face.
language.readingImpact: The detail reinforces the expectation of personal encounter and relational heat, in contrast to the distance caused by false masters.

language.title: "Deceivers" and "antichrist" as a severe language
language.detail: The note at 1:7 calls the masters deceivers and antichrist, using an apocalyptic symbol to mark the gravity of the error and the final judgment on them.
language.readingImpact: The letter does not treat heresy as secondary deviation; language intensifies the alert and guides the reader to see the error as spiritually dangerous.

timeline.title: The letter assumes the circulation of false masters in Asia Minor
timeline.detail: The introduction places the crisis in a period when itinerant teachers taught docetism and persuaded Christians to deny the reality of the body of Jesus.
timeline.readingImpact: The reading of the letter must be historical and pastoral: it responds to a concrete threat already in progress, not to an abstract theoretical discussion.

timeline.title: Separation of some members and training of an alternative group
timeline.detail: The introductory note states that some church members, influenced by false doctrine, broke with the community and formed a new sect.
timeline.readingImpact: This helps to understand the urgency of the tone: John writes to protect a community vulnerable to fragmentation.
timeline.reference: 2 John, general context of the introduction

timeline.title: Writing in apostolic context, with a planned future visit
timeline.detail: The letter closes with the promise of a brief visit by John and greetings from another community, showing a moment of living contact between churches.
timeline.readingImpact: The text is best read as a locationed correspondence, connected to a real network of churches and an active leader.

timeline.title: Extreme short of the epistle
timeline.detail: The introduction notes that the letter has only thirteen verses and would fit on a papyrus leaf.
timeline.readingImpact: The temporal scale of the composition seems short and functional: the epistolary genus allows immediate intervention in a specific crisis.

timeline.title: Primitive post-evangelical frame without exact date in sources
timeline.detail: The sources treat the letter as belonging to the period of the first churches, when several epistles were written to confront heretical teachings.
timeline.readingImpact: The reader should keep the chronology wide: the letter is old enough to dialogue with the formation and defense of apostolic teaching, but the notes do not provide precise date.

investigation: The sources clearly hold that the central problem is the presence of false masters/docetists in Asia Minor, but do not detail a precise external chronology.
The identification of the elected time with a concrete woman or with a local church remains debated in the notes; both readings appear, without final historical decision.
Matthew Henry emphasizes the dignity of a female recipient, but this line is devotional and does not add independent historical data beyond the possibility of a real woman.
The notes do not provide civil rulers, empires, absolute dates or economic details; therefore the policy section is necessarily limited.
Most of the backdrop comes from Tyndale, who reads 2 John in continuity with 1 John and with false teaching crises in the first churches.
The safest cultural framework is that of domestic communities, missionary hospitality and concern for doctrinal fidelity in the context of internal conflict.
dossier.limits: This dossier depends solely on the attached notes and is therefore selective. The sources well cover the doctrinal conflict, the hospitality in homes, the language of truth and love, and the possible identity of the recipient, but do not offer data on rulers, empires, broad economy or exact dates. Nor should the scenario narrated be confused with the date of composition: the letter takes place in a network of churches of Asia Minor under crisis of false masters, but the notes do not date the writing accurately. There is also a legitimate controversy over whether the elected "auticum" is an individual woman or a personified church; the sources hold both possibilities, although Tyndale considers the second most likely. Finally, references to docetism, Gnosticism and apostolic authorship appear as explanations of the notes, not as independent historical demonstrations.
